question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Dutch architectural and cultural legacy in Indian cities]
options: Chinsurah (Chinsura) — Dutch colonial buildings and the Dutch Cemetery survive in this Bengal town
Cochin (Fort Kochi) — Dutch Palace (Mattancherry Palace) built by the Dutch and given to the Raja of Cochin
Nagapattinam — Site of the Dutch Fort Vijfhoek on the Coromandel Coast
Surat — Dutch colonial capital in India where the VOC built its largest fort and administrative headquarters
wrong_fact: Surat was NOT the Dutch colonial capital nor the site of the VOC's largest fort in India. Surat was primarily an English and Mughal trading centre. The Dutch colonial capital and main administrative centre in India was Cochin (on the Malabar Coast) and later Nagapattinam (on the Coromandel Coast). The English had their first factory in Surat (1608).
explanation: Chinsurah (Bengal) has genuine Dutch heritage including the Dutch Cemetery. The Mattancherry Palace in Fort Kochi is popularly called the 'Dutch Palace' (though actually built by the Portuguese and renovated by the Dutch). Nagapattinam had Dutch Fort Vijfhoek. Surat, however, was the site of the first English factory in India and a major Mughal port — it was not a Dutch colonial capital or the location of the VOC's largest Indian fort.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Dutch impact on Indian naval and military technology]
options: Eustachius De Lannoy — Dutch naval officer who trained the Travancore navy after capture at Colachel (1741)
Travancore — Kingdom that built a modern navy partly with Dutch expertise after Battle of Colachel
Anjengo (Anchu Thengu) — Fort where Dutch prisoners were initially held after the Battle of Colachel
Musket and cannon technology — De Lannoy introduced Dutch gunnery and naval construction methods to Travancore
wrong_fact: Anjengo (Anchu Thengu) was actually a British East India Company fort on the Malabar Coast, not the place where Dutch prisoners from Colachel were held. Dutch prisoners including De Lannoy were taken inland to Travancore — De Lannoy eventually served the Travancore kingdom directly, not confined to Anjengo.
explanation: Eustachius De Lannoy was indeed a Dutch naval commander captured at Colachel who went on to modernise the Travancore navy. He trained Travancore in Dutch gunnery and shipbuilding. Anjengo (Anchu Thengu) was an English EIC fort in Kerala — it was not the Dutch prisoner camp. De Lannoy was taken to the Travancore court and served Marthanda Varma directly.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Dutch cartographic and geographic contributions relating to the Indian Ocean world]
options: Jan Huyghen van Linschoten — Dutch traveller whose 'Itinerario' (1596) gave Europeans access to Portuguese sea-route knowledge
Blaeu Atlas — Dutch cartographic work of the 17th century that included detailed maps of Asia and Indian Ocean trade routes
Cape of Good Hope — Charted and mapped extensively by Dutch navigators; Bartolomeu Dias named it but VOC perfected its navigation
Malabar Coast — First accurately mapped and charted by Dutch VOC cartographers; Portuguese maps of this coast were entirely discarded
wrong_fact: It is incorrect that Portuguese maps of the Malabar Coast were 'entirely discarded' and that the Dutch were the first to accurately map it. The Portuguese had extensively mapped the Malabar Coast through the early 16th century (Vasco da Gama's voyages, 1498 onward). Dutch cartographers built upon and refined existing Portuguese and Arab knowledge, not replaced them from scratch.
explanation: Linschoten's 'Itinerario' was genuinely pivotal in giving Dutch and English navigators access to Portuguese route knowledge. The Blaeu family's atlases (Joan Blaeu's 'Atlas Maior', 1662) included superb Asian and Indian Ocean maps. The Cape of Good Hope was indeed a Dutch navigational centre point (Dias named it 1488; Dutch mastered its use). However, the Malabar Coast was NOT first mapped by Dutch; Portuguese cartography from the early 1500s (Cantino planisphere, etc.) already documented it accurately. Dutch maps improved on, not replaced, Portuguese geographic knowledge.
